title: When to Migrate From QuickBooks to NetSuite: A Decision Framework
summary: QuickBooks to NetSuite migration decoded. See the real triggers, 2026 license and implementation costs, the 3 to 6 month timeline, and when to wait.
body_markdown:
## The Structural Difference


QuickBooks Online and NetSuite aren’t two rungs on the same ladder. They’re two different data models, which is the real reason a migration is a project rather than an export and an import.


Most comparison content treats this as a feature gap. It isn’t. A migration isn’t a software purchase. It’s a redesign of how your business gets measured.


- **QuickBooks Online is a single-company ledger.** Every QBO subscription maps to exactly one company file, with no native mechanism to combine two files into one consolidated trial balance and no intercompany elimination engine. Teams running more than one entity export each one separately, normalize charts of accounts that have drifted apart, convert currency by hand, and reassemble the consolidation every period.
- **NetSuite is a multi-subsidiary ledger.** In[NetSuite OneWorld](https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/netsuite/ns-online-help/section_N268563.html) , subsidiaries are records inside one account rather than separate accounts. Oracle documents dedicated[elimination subsidiaries](https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/netsuite/ns-online-help/section_N268759.html) and an[Automated Intercompany Management](https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/netsuite/ns-online-help/section_N1486610.html) feature that generates elimination journal entries for transaction lines flagged for elimination. The consolidation becomes a report run, not a monthly spreadsheet build.
- **The segment model is the piece migrations underestimate.** QBO carries dimensionality through classes and locations, unlimited on Advanced (Source:[Intuit, QuickBooks Online Advanced features](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/accounting/advanced-features/) , accessed July 2026). NetSuite carries it through subsidiary, department, class, location, and custom segments applied at the transaction line. The accounts you created to fake dimensionality, the ones named “Engineering Payroll” and “Sales Payroll,” collapse into one account plus a department segment. That’s why the chart of accounts gets redesigned rather than migrated.
- **Revenue recognition is the other structural gap.** QBO Advanced does include revenue recognition, and it’s worth being precise about what it does. Per[Intuit’s own help documentation](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/learn-support/en-us/help-article/accounting-method/understand-revenue-recognition-quickbooks-online/L9vA8v2qt_US_en_US) , it supports straight-line recognition calculated evenly across periods or by days in period, configured per product or service. That covers a clean annual subscription. It doesn’t cover standalone selling price allocation across a multi-element arrangement, usage-based revenue, or mid-term contract modifications, which is where[ASC 606 revenue recognition](https://www.indinero.com/blog/asc-606-what-you-need-to-know/) gets expensive. NetSuite handles those through[Advanced Revenue Management](https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/netsuite/ns-online-help/chapter_4328435538.html) , a rule-based framework for forecasting, recognition, reclassification, and deferral.
- **QBO has no sandbox.** NetSuite offers a purchasable test environment where configuration changes and integrations are validated before they touch production. For a company approaching a first financial statement audit, the absence of a test environment and a documented change process is a control gap an auditor will eventually name.


## Feature Comparison


The useful question isn’t which product has more features. It’s which capability QBO no longer delivers for you, and whether that capability is load-bearing.


Seven triggers show up repeatedly in growth-stage SaaS migrations. Each one has an observable signal you can check this week, and each one carries a different level of urgency.


Migration trigger Observable signal Urgency


A second entity needing consolidated statements The consolidated P&L is built in Excel, takes half a day, and one person owns it High when entities are material and audited


Revenue that stops recognizing on a straight line The deferred revenue waterfall breaks every time a customer upgrades mid-term High before a first audit or a Series C


Multi-currency beyond the occasional invoice A foreign subsidiary with its own functional currency, not just a customer paying in EUR High once statutory filing starts


User seats and permissions You’re rationing seats, or you’ve granted access you’re not comfortable with Low on its own


Close cycle time Close runs past ten calendar days, and the extra days are spent assembling data Depends entirely on the diagnosis


Investor and audit reporting An investor asks for a metric the system can’t produce without a manual build High when an audit lands inside 12 months


Integration sprawl and volume More than five systems write to the ledger, and reconciliation is a named job Moderate, often fixable


**The two triggers that carry the decision.** Multi-entity consolidation and non-straight-line revenue are the only two that justify the move on their own. QBO has no native consolidation and no automated eliminations, so every elimination is identified, calculated, and posted by hand outside the platform. Bolt-on reporting tools handle two or three entities acceptably. Past roughly four, or the moment eliminations become material to the reported number, the spreadsheet stops being a report and becomes a control weakness.


**The trigger everyone misreads.** Close cycle time gets used as the migration argument far more often than it should. APQC’s cross-industry benchmark, covering roughly 2,300 organizations, puts top-quartile monthly close at 4.8 calendar days or less, the median at 6.4 days, and the bottom quartile at ten days or more (Source:[CFO.com, “Metric of the Month: Cycle Time for Monthly Close”](https://www.cfo.com/news/metric-of-the-month-cycle-time-for-monthly-close/659297/) ). A close that runs long because of late vendor invoices, an unstaffed AP function, or no close checklist will still run long in NetSuite. Time-motion the close before you buy anything, and read the[signs your startup is ready for an ERP system](https://www.indinero.com/blog/startup-erp-systems/) as a diagnosis, not a shopping list.


**The honesty check.** As of July 2026, QBO Advanced gives you unlimited chart of accounts, unlimited classes and locations, 25 users, 48 custom fields, workflow automation with approval routing, batch transactions, straight-line revenue recognition, and, from August 2026, bundled Workforce Elite payroll and Bill Pay Elite (Source:[Intuit product update](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/r/product-update/quickbooks-price-changes/) , effective August 1, 2026). That’s a genuinely capable ledger. Plenty of single-entity SaaS companies at $15M ARR run on it well.


## Pricing Comparison


The cost of a QuickBooks to NetSuite migration is three numbers, not one. The license delta, the implementation fee, and the internal time nobody puts in the budget.


### The license delta


Start with the number the rest of the internet still has wrong. Intuit announced a price change effective August 1, 2026 for renewals on or after that date, affecting Essentials, Plus, and Advanced (Source:[Intuit, QuickBooks Online August pricing changes](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/r/product-update/quickbooks-price-changes/) , corroborated by[Certum Solutions](https://www.certumsolutions.com/library/quickbooks-price-increase-august-2026) ).


Plan Before Aug 1, 2026 Effective Aug 1, 2026 Users


Simple Start $38/mo $38/mo 1


Essentials $75/mo $85/mo 3


Plus $115/mo $140/mo 5


Advanced $275/mo $340/mo 25


Advanced carries the largest increase because Intuit is folding Workforce Elite payroll and Bill Pay Elite into it at no added subscription fee. New subscribers don’t see the increase until their seventh invoice. Even at $340/mo, QBO Advanced is $4,080 a year, and a QBO-anchored stack with a revenue subledger and a consolidation layer bolted on rarely clears $25,000 a year in software.


NetSuite is a different exercise, because Oracle publishes no NetSuite price list. Every quote is negotiated, so every figure below is a third-party reported range rather than a vendor price. Independent pricing trackers put base platform entry near $999/mo, rising to $5,000/mo and above by edition and service tier, with full user licenses reported at $99 to $199 per user per month and the standard full-user rate moved from $99 to $129. OneWorld is reported at $999 to $2,499/mo with each additional subsidiary adding roughly $500 to $1,000/mo, and advanced revenue recognition at $499 to $999/mo (Source:[ERP Research, Oracle NetSuite pricing, 2026](https://www.erpresearch.com/pricing/oracle-netsuite) ). For a two-entity, 12-user SaaS company running OneWorld and advanced revenue management, those reported ranges build to roughly $54,000 to $78,000 a year. Against $4,080 for QBO Advanced, that’s a recurring delta of $50,000 to $75,000 every year, not a one-time hit.


One more line to negotiate at signature rather than at renewal. NetSuite contracts commonly auto-renew with notice windows in the 60 to 90 day range, and reported annual uplift runs roughly 7% to 12% absent negotiation, steeper where the initial term was deeply discounted (Source:[Redress Compliance, NetSuite pricing negotiation, 2026](https://redresscompliance.com/netsuite-pricing-negotiation) ). Cap the uplift in writing. Diary the cancellation notice date the week you sign.


### The implementation fee


Reported implementation ranges for QBO to NetSuite specifically converge tightly. Independent guides put a standard implementation at $30,000 to $50,000, rising to $150,000 or more for complex multi-entity configurations (Source:[Ordway, “Migrating QuickBooks to NetSuite,” 2026](https://ordwaylabs.com/blog/migrating-from-quickbooks-online-to-netsuite-erp/) ), with a second implementer reporting the same low end and $120,000 to $150,000 and above at the complex end (Source:[Anchor Group, QuickBooks to NetSuite Migration Guide](https://www.anchorgroup.tech/blog/quick-books-netsuite-migration) ). Broader NetSuite implementations span $25,000 to $750,000, with typical mid-market landing at $75,000 to $250,000 and fixed-scope SuiteSuccess packages starting near $25,000 (Source: ERP Research, 2026).


Underneath those ranges sit partner hourly rates of $150 to $350 per hour, customization at $150 to $300 per hour, integrations from $0 to $7,500 one-time, and training at $2,000 to $15,000 one-time (Source:[CrossCountry Consulting, NetSuite Pricing Guide, February 2026](https://www.crosscountry-consulting.com/about-us/strategic-alliances/netsuite/pricing-guide/) ). The working heuristic partners use is 1.5x to 3x your first-year license fee. A fixed-fee quote issued before a structured discovery isn’t a real number.


### The internal time nobody budgets


This line item appears on no invoice and is frequently the largest one. A three to six month migration realistically consumes 15 to 25 hours a week from your controller or VP Finance during scoping, chart of accounts design, data validation, and parallel run. That’s roughly half a headcount for a quarter or two. Add 10 to 15 hours a week from a staff accountant during data cleansing and cutover, training time for every ledger-touching employee, and one to two months of closing the books in two systems at once.


At a fully loaded $110 an hour for a controller, 20 hours a week for 20 weeks is about $44,000 of cost that never gets quoted. For context on what that does to your run rate, SaaS Capital’s March 2026 survey of more than 1,000 private B2B SaaS companies puts median G&A spend at 15% of ARR, and 20% for equity-backed companies (Source:[SaaS Capital, 2026 Spending Benchmarks](https://www.saas-capital.com/blog-posts/spending-benchmarks-for-private-b2b-saas-companies/) ). A migration pushes a finance function well past its steady-state allocation. Plan for it or backfill for it.


### Year one, all in


The table below is for one specific profile. A two-entity, 12-user SaaS company running OneWorld and advanced revenue management. It is not a universal number, and a single-entity company with 6 users lands materially lower.


Line Low High


NetSuite license, year one $54,000 $78,000


Implementation, partner-led $45,000 $150,000


Integrations and connectors $5,000 $20,000


Training $2,000 $15,000


Internal time, unbudgeted $40,000 $90,000


Year-one all in $146,000 $353,000


Less QBO stack retired ($10,000) ($30,000)


Years two and beyond are license plus 7% to 12% uplift, plus whatever ongoing partner support you retain. If that build-up makes you want a second opinion on the whole category, our overview of[enterprise accounting software](https://www.indinero.com/blog/best-enterprise-accounting-software/) covers the alternatives worth pricing.


## When to Choose QuickBooks Online


Stay on QuickBooks Online when your complexity is process complexity rather than structural complexity. That distinction decides the entire question, and a $150,000 ERP project fixes only one of the two.


Stay put if all six of these are true:


1. **One legal entity, or a second one that’s immaterial.** A dormant holdco or a foreign R&D subsidiary with fewer than 50 transactions a month needs a clean intercompany agreement and a monthly journal entry, not OneWorld.
2. **Revenue recognizes ratably.** Annual and monthly subscriptions, no usage tiers, no bundled implementation services requiring allocation, no material mid-term amendments.
3. **One functional currency.** Foreign customers paying in their own currency is a transaction problem, not a translation problem, and QBO handles it from the Essentials tier up.
4. **Close runs under eight calendar days and the constraint isn’t the system.** The median across APQC’s benchmark set is 6.4 days (Source: CFO.com citing APQC). At 6 days, a new ERP buys you very little.
5. **Fewer than 25 people need ledger access.**
6. **No audit inside 12 months, or an audit you’ve already passed on the current stack.**


### The genuine “not yet” cases


**You’re under $5M ARR with simple operations.** Independent cost analysis is blunt here. A 10-person company at $1M revenue with straightforward operations will spend $50,000 or more in year one on a platform built for complexity it doesn’t have, and most NetSuite customers sit in the $10M to $500M revenue band (Source:[ERP Research, 2026](https://www.erpresearch.com/pricing/oracle-netsuite) ).


**Your complexity is temporary.** An acquisition you’ll fully integrate within nine months, a single enterprise contract with unusual terms, a currency exposure from one customer. Don’t build permanent infrastructure for a temporary condition.


**You don’t have the internal capacity.** A migration run by a finance team that’s already underwater produces a badly configured NetSuite instance, which is worse than a well-configured QBO instance. If your controller is the only person who knows how the books work, fix that first. The bus factor is one.


**You’re mid-fundraise, mid-audit, or in your fiscal fourth quarter.** Cutting over during peak season is a named failure mode. So is cutting over while a diligence team is in the data room.


**You haven’t fixed your chart of accounts.** If the COA is a mess in QBO, migrating hands the mess to a more expensive system. Rebuilding it in QBO first is cheap, reversible, and delivers most of the reporting benefit people believe they’re buying from NetSuite.


### Price the bridge before you price the project


Three configurations buy real runway, and they belong on the table alongside any NetSuite quote:


- **QBO Advanced plus a revenue subledger.** Maxio is commonly used, priced from roughly $599/mo for up to $100,000 in monthly billing volume, with the recognition module as a paid add-on (Source:[ScaleXP, Maxio pricing for $5M to $20M ARR finance teams](https://www.scalexp.com/maxio-pricing-what-finance-teams-at-5m-20m-arr-actually-pay/) ). Verify the journal-entry write-back path before you buy. That’s the common failure point.
- **QBO Advanced plus a consolidation reporting layer.** Workable for two to four entities for reporting purposes. It doesn’t deliver statutory or audit-grade elimination, so treat it as a runway extender rather than a fix.
- **A mid-market ERP that isn’t NetSuite.** Sage Intacct is built around multi-entity consolidation and native ASC 606, and typically implements faster and cheaper for a finance-only scope. If you have no inventory, no manufacturing, and no commerce, the full suite may be more platform than the problem requires. Our comparison of[cloud-based accounting platforms](https://www.indinero.com/blog/cloud-based-accounting-platforms/) is a reasonable starting point.


A partner whose revenue depends on the implementation proceeding has no structural reason to price those three options for you. That’s not a criticism of partners. It’s just how the incentive runs.


## When to Choose NetSuite


Migrate when two or more structural triggers are true at the same time, and at least one of them is multi-entity consolidation or revenue recognition. The migrate-now signal set:


1. **Two or more material legal entities requiring consolidated, audited statements with intercompany eliminations.** The strongest single trigger. It can justify the move under $5M revenue on its own.
2. **Revenue contracts that break straight-line recognition.** Multi-element bundles requiring allocation, usage-based revenue, or routine mid-term modifications.
3. **Multiple functional currencies with statutory filing obligations.**
4. **A first financial statement audit inside 12 months on a ledger that’s never been audited.** Auditors test the revenue number hardest, and a spreadsheet waterfall is the finding you don’t want in year one. Our guide to[audit preparation](https://www.indinero.com/blog/audit-preparation/) covers what that testing actually looks like.
5. **Close consistently past ten calendar days for system reasons** , verified by an actual time-motion study rather than a feeling. Bottom-quartile close in APQC’s benchmark set is ten days or more (Source: CFO.com citing APQC).
6. **Transaction volume past roughly 50,000 lines a year** , with reconciliation between systems now somebody’s named responsibility.
7. **An acquisition strategy.** If the operating plan includes buying companies, buy the ledger that can absorb them before the first close, not after.


### The revenue band, stated honestly


Published guidance clusters across a wide range because revenue is a proxy, not a cause. One implementer puts the evaluation window at $5M to $10M with the practical trigger at $10M and above (Source: Ordway, 2026). Another places the typical band at roughly $10M to $50M while stating plainly that structural factors matter more than revenue (Source:[EPIQ, QuickBooks to NetSuite Migration guide, 2026](https://epiqinfo.com/quickbooks-to-netsuite-migration/) ). ERP Research places most NetSuite customers in the $10M to $500M band.


Here’s how we’d frame it instead. A single-entity SaaS company recognizing ratably can run cleanly to $15M or $20M ARR on QBO Advanced. A two-entity SaaS company with a foreign sub and enterprise contracts is straining at $4M. Structure, not revenue, sets the ceiling.


The best time to start is six to twelve months before the constraint becomes binding. A migration run under duress, during an audit or a fundraise or a year-end, is the one that overruns. If you can see the second entity coming, start scoping while your team still has slack. Companies[scaling from small business to enterprise accounting](https://www.indinero.com/blog/scaling-from-small-business-to-enterprise-accounting/) almost always wish they had started the conversation two quarters earlier.


## Implementation Considerations


Three to six months from kickoff to go-live is the consistent published range for a QuickBooks Online to NetSuite migration (Sources: Ordway 2026, EPIQ 2026).


### The realistic timeline


Broken down by company size, published guidance puts small businesses at three to four months, mid-market at four to six, and enterprise at six to twelve or more, with the data migration workstream running roughly eight weeks inside that (Source:[Anchor Group](https://www.anchorgroup.tech/blog/quick-books-netsuite-migration) ). Oracle’s accelerated methodology, SuiteSuccess, targets a baseline go-live near 100 days using pre-configured industry editions with prebuilt roles, dashboards, and workflows. Read that number carefully. It’s the methodology’s stated target for a leading-practice baseline configuration, not a fully integrated finish line, and real projects are commonly described in the 100 to 140 day range.


Phase Duration What actually happens


Requirements scoping and discovery 4 to 6 weeks Process mapping, entity structure, revenue policy documentation, integration inventory. The phase teams compress and then pay for later.


Chart of accounts and segment design 2 to 3 weeks Redesign, not lift and shift. Decide what’s an account versus a department, class, location, or custom segment.


Data extraction and cleansing 3 to 5 weeks Customer and vendor deduplication, item normalization, open transaction validation, deferred revenue reconstruction.


Configuration and first trial load 3 to 4 weeks Sandbox configuration, first data load, mapping error discovery.


Integration build 3 to 6 weeks, parallel Billing or Stripe, Bill.com, payroll, expense, CRM, BI. Runs alongside configuration.


Second trial load and validation 2 to 3 weeks The load that catches what the first one missed. Skipping it is a named pitfall.


Parallel run 4 to 8 weeks Close in both systems. One to two full cycles.


Cutover and stabilization 2 to 4 weeks Go-live, first solo close, issue triage.


### What migrates and what gets rebuilt


Object Treatment Why


Chart of accounts Redesigned, not copied Copying the legacy COA forfeits the segment reporting you’re paying for.


Customers, vendors, items Migrated after cleansing Deduplication happens before load. That’s billable time or your team’s time.


Open AR and open AP Migrated at detail Operational continuity. Every open invoice and bill comes across.


Trial balance Migrated as opening balances Typically as of the cutover period close.


Deferred revenue schedules Migrated as opening balances Open subscription balances become NetSuite opening[deferred revenue](https://www.indinero.com/blog/the-key-to-accrual-accounting-recording-deferred-revenue/) . Highest-risk object in a SaaS migration.


Historical transaction detail 1 to 3 years, or summarized Full history multiplies effort for little return.


Older closed-period detail Summarized or archived Keep QBO read-only for a retention period, or export to a warehouse.


Bank feeds and payroll connection Reconfigured fresh Not migratable. Re-establish and re-map to the new COA.


Custom reports and saved searches Rebuilt QBO report definitions don’t translate to the new segment model.


Workflows and approvals Redesigned, not replicated Recreating QBO workflows reproduces the constraints you were escaping.


User roles and permissions Rebuilt NetSuite’s role model is far more detailed. Design it deliberately.


### What makes a project slip


1. **Under-scoping requirements.** The most common and most expensive failure. Discovery gets compressed to two weeks to hit a budget, and the missing scope surfaces during the parallel run when change orders cost the most.
2. **Copying the legacy chart of accounts.** Locks your old workarounds into a more expensive system.
3. **Migrating bad data.** Partners load data. They don’t fix it. Duplicate customers, stale vendors, and inconsistent item naming arrive intact unless somebody cleans them first.
4. **A single trial load.** One load hides mapping errors. Two loads find them while there’s still time.
5. **Migrating complete history.** Multiplies cost and elapsed time for records almost nobody queries after go-live.
6. **Skipping or shortening the parallel run.** The parallel close is the only real test. Four weeks saved here becomes four weeks of re-closing later.
7. **Under-investing in training.** Adoption failure looks exactly like software failure from the outside. Budget the $2,000 to $15,000 line.
8. **Cutting over during peak season, year-end, or an audit.**
9. **No named internal owner with decision authority.** A migration without a decision-maker inside the company becomes a sequence of change orders.


Panorama Consulting’s 2026 ERP Report found that more than a quarter of organizations exceeded their project budget, with additional technology needs the leading cause (Source:[Panorama Consulting Group, March 2026](https://www.panorama-consulting.com/panorama-consulting-group-releases-latest-study-of-erp-implementation-outcomes-across-the-globe/) ). Note the direction of that finding. The overrun driver is usually scope discovered late, not partners overcharging.


### Do you need a NetSuite partner


For the build, effectively yes. NetSuite is delivered through Oracle professional services or through solution provider and alliance partners, and reviewers consistently flag that it requires significant configuration out of the box, which means internal technical resources or outside consultants (Source:[G2, NetSuite reviews](https://www.g2.com/products/netsuite/reviews) ). What’s worth separating is who advises you on whether to migrate, and who owns your accounting afterward. A partner whose revenue depends on the implementation happening isn’t structurally positioned to tell you not to do it. That separation is the whole argument for a tool-neutral advisor on the decision and the design, with a certified partner on the build.


## How Indinero Implements NetSuite or QBO


Indinero isn’t a NetSuite reseller and takes no software margin, which is why “not yet, here’s the eighteen-month bridge” is an answer we can actually give.


A QBO to NetSuite migration is the defining systems event in the transition zone between AI bookkeeping plus one CPA and GAAP-clean books plus a first audit plus multi-state nexus. It rarely arrives alone. It usually lands in the same year as the first audit, the first serious R&D credit claim, and a 409A cadence, and those events all draw on the same underlying data. Running them through one finance function instead of four vendors is the practical argument, not a philosophical one.


What the engagement looks like:


1. **A readiness diagnostic before anything is purchased.** Time-motion the close and identify which days are system-caused. Map the entity structure and the real materiality of each entity. Review the contract book against the straight-line boundary in QBO Advanced. Count the reconciliation surfaces. The deliverable is a migrate-now, migrate-later, or don’t-migrate recommendation with evidence attached.
2. **Chart of accounts and segment design before partner selection.** This is the highest-leverage decision in the project and the one most often handed to whoever is cheapest. We design it against SaaS reporting requirements first, so the P&L supports ARR, gross margin by revenue stream, contribution margin by department, and a revenue waterfall that survives audit.
3. **A requirements document partners bid against.** A specified scope is what turns an open-ended project into a bounded one. Ambiguity is the most expensive thing in an ERP contract.
4. **Data cleansing on the QBO side, before extraction.** Deduplicate customers and vendors, normalize items, reconstruct deferred revenue schedules, validate the trial balance. Cleaning at accounting rates costs less than cleaning at partner rates of $150 to $350 an hour (Source: CrossCountry Consulting, February 2026).
5. **A parallel run that’s actually staffed.** Closing in two systems for one to two cycles takes roughly double the close labor, which is exactly why the parallel run gets cut. We staff the second close so it doesn’t.
6. **Integrations and the reporting layer.** Billing, Stripe, Bill.com, expense, payroll, and CRM into the ledger, and the ledger into dashboards. Our[technology and business intelligence services](https://www.indinero.com/services/technology-business-intelligence-services/) cover this on both platforms, including multi-entity consolidation and budget-versus-actual reporting.
7. **The QBO path when migration isn’t the answer.** Same team, different work. Rebuild the COA in QBO, automate the close checklist, add a revenue subledger where straight line breaks, and build the consolidation and dashboard layer. Most of the reporting outcome, a fraction of the cost, migration deferred until it’s genuinely load-bearing.


None of this sits beside your accounting. Bookkeeping, accounting, tax, and fractional CFO advisory are bundled under one monthly engagement, so the people designing your chart of accounts are the same people closing your books on it and the same people building the[board reporting](https://www.indinero.com/services/cfo-services/) that runs on top. Indinero has maintained continuous operations since 2009 and works with 500+ regular customers, which means the team that scopes your migration is the team still supporting the ledger three years later.


The move to NetSuite is right for some growth-stage SaaS companies and premature for many more. If you can’t tell which one you are, that’s the conversation to have before you sign a license.


## Frequently asked questions


Common questions about QuickBooks to NetSuite migration timing, cost, scope, and what stays behind in QBO.


### What signs say a SaaS company has outgrown QuickBooks Online?


A SaaS company has outgrown QuickBooks Online when a second material entity needs consolidated statements or revenue contracts stop recognizing on a straight line. Those two carry the decision on their own, and secondary signals include a foreign functional currency, a close consistently past ten calendar days for system reasons, and a first audit inside 12 months. Indinero treats two or more of these together, with at least one being structural, as the actual signal to migrate.


### How much does a typical QBO to NetSuite migration cost?


Implementation partners report $30,000 to $50,000 for a straightforward QBO to NetSuite migration, rising past $150,000 for complex multi-entity configurations. License sits on top of that, and Oracle publishes no NetSuite price list, so every figure is a negotiated quote against third-party reported ranges. Indinero budgets the controller hours too, which is why year one all in for a two-entity, 12-user SaaS company lands near $146,000 to $353,000.


### How long does a NetSuite implementation actually take?


Three to six months from kickoff to go-live is the consistent published range for a QuickBooks Online to NetSuite migration. Oracle’s SuiteSuccess methodology targets a baseline go-live near 100 days, but that’s the methodology’s stated target for a leading-practice configuration, not a fully integrated finish line. The phases that slip are discovery, which gets compressed to hit a budget, and the parallel run, which indinero staffs precisely because capacity pressure is what kills it.


### What gets migrated and what gets recreated in NetSuite?


Balances and cleansed master data migrate to NetSuite, while the chart of accounts, reports, workflows, integrations, and user roles get redesigned or rebuilt. Migrated objects include open AR and AP at detail, the trial balance as opening balances, deduplicated customers and vendors, and one to three years of active history. Deferred revenue schedules are the highest-risk object in a SaaS migration, so indinero reconstructs and reconciles them in QBO before extraction rather than after load.


### Can a company stay on QBO past $10M revenue with workarounds?


Yes, a single-entity SaaS company with one functional currency and ratable revenue can run cleanly on QuickBooks Online Advanced to $15M or $20M ARR. Intuit raises Advanced from $275 to $340 a month on August 1, 2026, and even then the license is $4,080 a year. Indinero isn’t a NetSuite reseller, so the bridge stack of a revenue subledger plus a consolidation layer is an answer we can honestly recommend. The workarounds stop working when eliminations become material or a foreign functional currency arrives.


### Does NetSuite implementation require hiring a NetSuite consultant?


For the build, effectively yes, because NetSuite is delivered through Oracle professional services or certified partners and needs significant configuration out of the box. The real question is scope. A company with a strong controller and a clean requirements document can run a much lighter partner engagement than a default fixed-fee package. Indinero separates the decision and the design from the build, since a partner whose revenue depends on the migration proceeding isn’t positioned to tell you not to.


### What are the most common NetSuite implementation mistakes?


Under-scoping requirements is the most common and most expensive NetSuite implementation mistake, followed by copying the legacy chart of accounts instead of redesigning it. Others repeat constantly. Migrating dirty data, running a single trial load, loading complete history, shortening the parallel run, under-budgeting training, and cutting over during year-end or an audit. The underlying cause is usually scope discovered late, which is why indinero writes the requirements document partners bid against before anyone selects one.
